newsitem.title: FRANCE: Foncier sit-in nears end before key talks.
newsitem.headline: Foncier sit-in nears end before key talks.

text.p: Staff protestors at French bank Credit Foncier are poised to end a sit-in after several weeks if a meeting later on Wednesday wins them more time to save the institution from break-up.

A trade union source said staff could end the "occupation", which began on January 17, if the government agreed to change the bank's statutes, which would allow more time to repair its balance sheet after huge 1995 losses.

Le Monde newspaper said a report by Paribas bank had confirmed the possibility of Foncier making a profit of more than one billion francs ($170 million) this year but said that it could need a recapitalisation of up to six billion francs.
The Wednesday meeting of shareholders was slated to start at 1500 GMT.
The union source said talks with a government-appointed mediator were continuing, as staff sought alternatives to a plan announced by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis in July.
The Arthuis plan calls for a partial takeover of the bank and a wind-down of the rest.

"This will be the last day of our occupation but it does not mean we do not remain mobilised. We are still talking to the mediator," the source from a cross-union group at Foncier said, requesting anonymity.
But this did not mean a state plan to dismantle the bank had been shelved, and talks were continuing.
Staff occupying the Paris headquarters of the home loans group held its chairman hostage for six days to protest against the Arthuis plan.

Arthuis has already carried out the first stage by getting the state-owned bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations to "nationalise" Foncier through a buyout of shareholders for more than two billion francs.

The second stage would involve spinning off its property loans business to a rival, cooperatively run group called Credit Immobilier and shunting the rest into a state holding company to be shut down over time.

Credit Foncier, which was private but had top management named by the state as a "specialised financial institution" providing low-cost home loans, reported a 1995 loss of 10.8 billion francs in April.
Unions argue the losses were overstated to fell the group and that it could still be made viable despite misadventures in property in the past.

Under Credit Foncier's statutes, which are different from those of ordinary companies, the 145-year-old bank should have plugged its balance sheet within four months and has stayed in business only following the state-sponsored takeover.

Wednesday's meeting of shareholders was to decide whether the rules should be changed to allow Foncier up to two years to mend its finances, a technicality bringing the firm into line with ordinary company law but also giving it time to breathe.

The union source said the staff sit-in would be called off if, as expected, the legal resolution went through. But any hiccups at the meeting could see the protests expanded. ($ = 5.572 French Francs)
